description: Cosmic Coasters is a small club of space enthusiasts at our university of applied sciences Campus Vienna.
summary: We developed a browser-based tool for exploring SPHEREx observations in support of the search for Planet X. Users choose a sky position by entering right ascension and declination or selecting a point on an interactive globe. The application retrieves available SPHEREx observations for that region and turns them into color time-lapse animations, alongside difference views that make changes between visits easier to see. Timestamps and star overlays help users interpret interesting sources and follow up on what they find. By making repeated observations easy to compare, the project helps users visually investigate moving or changing objects that may merit further study. This matters because a distant, faint object could be overlooked in individual images; bringing archival observations into an approachable visual workflow can help more people explore the data, notice potential clues, and contribute to the broader investigation.
details:
PlanetX Finder is a browser-based tool for exploring observations from NASA's SPHEREx infrared space telescope. It turns observations of a selected region of the sky into a color time-lapse, helping users see how that region changes across different observation visits.

HOW IT WORKS

Users enter a sky position as Right Ascension and Declination, or select a position using the interactive celestial globe. The Python backend searches SPHEREx observation collections available through NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), finds images covering the selected position, and processes them into frames ordered by observation time.

The backend aligns and combines data from SPHEREx detectors into color images using a consistent brightness scale across frames. Blue represents detectors D1-D3 (0.75-2.4 micrometers), red represents detectors D4-D6 (2.4-5.0 micrometers), and green combines the red and blue channels. It also creates difference images by comparing each frame with a reference made from observations using the same detectors. These images help make changes between visits easier to notice.

The frontend displays the result as an animated GIF. Users can adjust the cutout size and animation speed, inspect difference images, and pause or step through frames.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The project makes archival infrared observations easier to explore without requiring users to process the raw data themselves. Presenting observations as a time-lapse and highlighting differences can help users notice moving or changing sources that may be difficult to spot in individual images.

PlanetX Finder is an exploratory aid, not a discovery-confirmation system. Its intended impact is to make SPHEREx data more approachable and support the identification of candidates for further investigation, including possible distant moving objects.

WHAT MAKES THE APPROACH CREATIVE

The project combines a coordinate-selectable celestial globe, multi-wavelength color imagery, and time-based difference images in one interactive experience. The globe lets users choose sky coordinates visually, while the paired time-lapse and difference views offer ways to inspect change across observations.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

The frontend uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in a web browser. It includes a canvas-based celestial globe and controls for coordinates and image playback.

The backend and middleware use Python. The backend uses Astropy, Astroquery, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, Requests, and Matplotlib for astronomical data access, image processing, and rendering. Observation searches use IRSA, Gaia and WISE, with the public SPHEREx AWS archive available as a data source.

The project runs as a local web application, with a Python HTTP server connecting the browser frontend to the processing backend.

WHAT FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

We considered usability, usefulness, accessibility, and performance. We also had to work around Caltech server limitations by storing part of the data in cache. The performance improved from 5 to 10 minutes to 20 to 30 seconds per run.

We oriented ourselves around DeepSkyStacker and a Zooniverse project. We looked at how DeepSkyStacker combines the raw images in such a way, that noise and artifacts don't show up in the final GIF, but fast moving objects, that could appear on only one frame, do show up.
